questions.title: Choledochal cyst and bilirubin metabolism
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Choledochal cyst and bilirubin metabolism

Bilirubin arises mainly from haem breakdown: haem oxygenase produces biliverdin, reduced to unconjugated bilirubin. Albumin carries it to the liver, UGT1A1 conjugates it, and canalicular transport excretes it into bile. Intestinal metabolism produces urobilinogen and faecal stercobilin; some undergoes enterohepatic circulation. Neonatal immaturity, haemolysis, breast-milk effects, hypothyroidism and conjugation disorders cause unconjugated jaundice; sepsis, BA, biliary cysts and hepatocellular/metabolic disease cause conjugated jaundice. Jaundice in the first day, rapid rise, prolonged jaundice, illness or conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia requires evaluation; pathological status is not defined by colour alone.

Todani types: I fusiform/cystic extrahepatic dilatation (subtypes Ia/Ib/Ic); II diverticulum; III choledochocele; IVa intra- and extrahepatic, IVb multiple extrahepatic; V Caroli disease. Draw normal ducts next to each schematic. Abnormal pancreaticobiliary junction and pancreatic reflux are important mechanisms, while developmental/obstructive factors also contribute. Forme-fruste disease has an abnormal junction and symptoms without striking duct dilatation.

Presentation includes neonatal cholestasis, pain, pancreatitis, cholangitis or a mass; the classic triad is uncommon. Ultrasound is initial imaging; MRCP defines biliary and pancreatic anatomy. Check liver tests, coagulation and pancreatic enzymes. In an infant, distinguish a cystic BA remnant from a communicating choledochal cyst before reconstruction.

For common extrahepatic types, complete cyst excision with cholecystectomy and a wide Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy is established treatment; hepaticoduodenostomy is an alternative with different reflux considerations. Carefully separate portal structures and define the distal intrapancreatic junction. Treat cholangitis/pancreatitis and correct vitamin-K-related coagulopathy before surgery where possible. Type II/III and intrahepatic disease need anatomy-specific treatment; diffuse Caroli disease with severe complications may require transplantation. Follow anastomotic stricture, stones, cholangitis, pancreatitis and residual malignancy risk; internal drainage without excision is not adequate definitive management for a usual type-I cyst.

### Neonatal cholestasis, biliary atresia and Kasai outcomes

### Recognition and investigation
Conjugated jaundice is pathological. Persistent jaundice, pale/acholic stools, dark urine and hepatomegaly warrant prompt direct bilirubin measurement and hepatobiliary assessment. A direct bilirubin above 1 mg/dL is an important abnormal threshold; the older requirement that it exceed 20% of total bilirubin can miss disease. Differential diagnosis includes biliary atresia, choledochal cyst, infection, alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, Alagille syndrome, metabolic/endocrine disorders, genetic bile-transport disease and parenteral-nutrition-associated cholestasis.

Assess stool colour, growth, bleeding and splenic/associated abnormalities. Tests include fractionated bilirubin, liver enzymes/GGT, albumin, glucose, INR (including response to vitamin K), CBC, cultures when needed and targeted metabolic/genetic investigations. Fasting ultrasound assesses gallbladder morphology, triangular-cord sign, ducts, cysts and vascular anatomy. No single negative ultrasound or scintigraphic result reliably excludes BA. Hepatobiliary scintigraphy can demonstrate excretion; absent excretion is nonspecific and must not delay definitive evaluation. Liver biopsy often shows bile duct proliferation, bile plugs, portal oedema and fibrosis. Intraoperative cholangiography establishes extrahepatic patency/anatomy when BA is suspected.

### Pathology and operation
BA is progressive fibro-obliterative cholangiopathy with interacting developmental, inflammatory and immune mechanisms. CMV-associated BA is a described subgroup; association does not prove CMV causes all BA, and antiviral treatment needs specialist selection. Anatomical types are I (common bile duct), II (common hepatic duct, with subtypes), and III (at porta hepatis; most common). A cystic hilar lesion may represent cystic BA rather than a patent choledochal cyst; assess distal patency and hepatic ducts.

Kasai hepatoportoenterostomy removes the fibrotic extrahepatic remnant and exposes microscopic ductules at the portal plate, connected to a Roux-en-Y jejunal limb. Earlier diagnosis and surgery improve the chance of bile drainage; age is not the sole criterion. Avoid damage to portal vessels and inappropriate deep excision. Provide high-energy nutrition, fat-soluble vitamins, cholangitis treatment and surveillance. The benefit of routine steroids is unsettled and protocol dependent.

### Prognosis and transplantation
Jaundice clearance and bilirubin after Kasai, age/fibrosis at operation, anatomical/syndromic disease, recurrent cholangitis, centre experience and portal hypertension influence native-liver survival. Some children retain native liver long term, while others develop cirrhosis despite initial bile drainage. Follow growth, fat-soluble vitamins, coagulopathy, varices, ascites, hepatopulmonary syndrome and malignancy surveillance where indicated. Refer early for transplant assessment after failed drainage, progressive decompensation, refractory portal-hypertension complications, severe growth failure or recurrent uncontrollable cholangitis. Kasai is a bridge to long-term native-liver health or transplantation, rather than a guaranteed cure.

![Original teaching schematic: todani. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/todani.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NASPGHAN/ESPGHAN infant cholestasis guideline](https://www.naspghan.org/files/documents/pdfs/position-papers/Guideline_for_the_Evaluation_of_Cholestatic.23.pdf)

questions.title: Germ-cell tumours, sacrococcygeal teratoma and testis preservation
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Germ-cell tumours, sacrococcygeal teratoma and testis preservation

Germ-cell tumours derive from primordial germ cells with gonadal or midline extragonadal sites. Histological types include mature/immature teratoma, yolk-sac (endodermal-sinus) tumour, seminomatous tumours, embryonal carcinoma and choriocarcinoma, often mixed. AFP supports yolk-sac differentiation and monitoring; beta-hCG supports trophoblastic components; LDH reflects burden in selected tumours. Interpret AFP against age because infants normally have high AFP. Failure of a marker to decline appropriately after treatment suggests residual disease, but use known biological half-life and age norms.

SCT Altman types: I predominantly external; II external with significant intrapelvic extension; III predominantly pelvic/abdominal with an external component; IV entirely presacral. Approximate historical distributions are about 45%, 35%, 10% and 10%, varying by series. Fetal prognosis depends on solid vascular mass, high-output failure, hydrops, tumour growth, prematurity and bleeding, rather than type alone. Ultrasound/echo and selected MRI guide monitoring and delivery. Surgical excision includes the coccyx, preserving pelvic nerves and sphincter function. Resect without spillage where feasible; malignant elements require oncology input. Follow serial age-adjusted AFP, imaging/clinical recurrence, continence and bowel/urinary function. Immature histology is not identical to malignant yolk-sac tumour.

Testicular masses need ultrasound and preoperative AFP/beta-hCG; assess puberty/age and metastatic staging according to pathology. A suspected malignant tumour generally requires inguinal exploration with cord control, avoiding transscrotal biopsy. Testis-sparing excision is considered for suitable prepubertal likely benign lesions when normal tissue can be preserved and reliable frozen/permanent pathology is available. Malignant germ-cell tumour commonly requires radical inguinal orchidectomy and protocol-specific chemotherapy/staging. Staging distinguishes disease confined to the gonad, retroperitoneal spread and distant metastases, but specify the paediatric protocol rather than importing adult staging uncritically.

Yolk-sac tumour shows AFP secretion, characteristic reticular morphology and possible Schiller-Duval bodies. Counsel about fertility/endocrine function and surveillance. Never infer a tumour is benign solely because it is painless or an ultrasound is cystic.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NCI PDQ: Childhood extracranial germ-cell tumours, professional version](https://www.cancer.gov/types/extracranial-germ-cell/hp/germ-cell-treatment-pdq)

questions.title: Non-Wilms renal tumours and small-round-cell diagnostics
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Non-Wilms renal tumours and small-round-cell diagnostics

Infant renal masses include congenital mesoblastic nephroma (CMN), Wilms tumour, rhabdoid tumour and less commonly other lesions. CMN is common in early infancy; classic and cellular forms have different biological behaviour, with ETV6-NTRK3 fusions characteristic of many cellular lesions. Nephrectomy with complete excision is usual management; selected higher-risk/recurrent cellular disease needs oncology treatment and molecularly directed options. Monitor recurrence according to pathology/stage rather than assuming every CMN is benign.

Clear-cell sarcoma of kidney is aggressive and can metastasise to bone and brain; BCOR alterations support diagnosis in many cases. Treat with complete surgical staging and protocol-specific multiagent chemotherapy/radiotherapy. Rhabdoid tumour often affects infants and shows loss of SMARCB1/INI1 expression (or less commonly SMARCA4 abnormalities); search for synchronous CNS disease and predisposition. Pediatric RCC occurs more in older children, including translocation-associated forms; treatment differs from Wilms chemotherapy.

Immunohistochemistry is interpreted as a panel alongside morphology, site, age and molecular tests. Examples: RMS desmin/myogenin/MyoD1; neuroblastoma neuronal/neuroendocrine markers and PHOX2B; Ewing sarcoma CD99/NKX2.2 with a defining fusion test; lymphoma lineage markers; rhabdoid INI1 loss; germ-cell tumours SALL4 and subtype markers; hepatoblastoma hepatocytic markers with other morphology-specific stains. A marker is not perfectly specific, so avoid diagnosing a 'small round blue cell tumour' from CD99 or desmin alone.

Molecular tests can establish fusions, refine risk and identify actionable targets, using FISH, RT-PCR or sequencing as appropriate. Obtain tissue with a planned biopsy route and enough material for histology and ancillary testing; avoid necrotic tissue and inappropriate decalcification. Communicate treatment history because preoperative chemotherapy changes tumour composition. Liquid biopsy of circulating tumour DNA/cells is promising for residual disease and genomic profiling but remains tumour- and assay-specific, and cannot universally replace tissue.

### Wilms tumour: staging, risk and nephron-sparing surgery

Wilms tumour is an embryonal renal malignancy with variable blastemal, epithelial and stromal components. Assess an abdominal mass without repeated vigorous palpation, BP, haematuria and syndromic features. Ultrasound and contrast cross-sectional imaging establish renal origin, contralateral disease, rupture and renal-vein/IVC thrombus; chest staging and protocol-specific laboratory assessment are required. Genetic predispositions include WT1-associated WAGR/Denys-Drash/Frasier spectra, 11p15-associated overgrowth/Beckwith-Wiedemann and other familial syndromes. Nephrogenic rests are persisting embryonal renal tissue: perilobar versus intralobar, with different associations; nephroblastomatosis indicates extensive/multiple rests.

NWTS/COG stages: I confined to kidney and completely excised; II beyond kidney but completely excised; III residual nonhaematogenous abdominal disease (including positive margins/nodes or qualifying spill/rupture/biopsy according to protocol); IV haematogenous or distant nodal metastases; V bilateral disease at diagnosis. Protocol definitions matter. COG commonly begins with nephrectomy in a suitable unilateral tumour; SIOP generally gives preoperative chemotherapy in typical cases. Do not mix the two systems' histology, biopsy/spill criteria or treatment schedules.

SIOP postchemotherapy histological risk broadly separates low-risk completely necrotic/certain differentiated lesions, intermediate-risk common subtypes and focal anaplasia, and high-risk blastemal-type/diffuse anaplastic disease, interpreted with staging and the current protocol. UMBRELLA integrates harmonised imaging, surgical/pathology review, molecular biology and risk-adapted treatment; it is more than a new staging table. Age, stage, histology, response, residual volume and molecular abnormalities such as adverse chromosomal changes influence prognosis.

For standard nephrectomy preserve tumour integrity, obtain adequate regional lymph-node samples even if nodes look normal, assess thrombus and avoid rupture. Nephron-sparing surgery is central for bilateral tumours, solitary kidneys and predisposition syndromes, and selected unilateral cases within appropriate protocols. Prerequisites include ability to achieve clear margins, viable renal remnant with preserved inflow/outflow, accurate mapping and expert pathology/oncology support. Multifocal distribution, unfavourable anatomy or inability to obtain safe complete excision can preclude it. Bilateral disease usually receives preoperative chemotherapy with planned renal-preserving operations, avoiding indefinite chemotherapy without reassessment.

Map caval thrombus extent and vascular anatomy; supradiaphragmatic/atrial extension may require cardiac support. Preoperative chemotherapy can reduce thrombus in suitable protocol settings. Obtain proximal/distal vascular control, avoid fragmentation and embolisation, and perform thrombectomy with selected vascular reconstruction; refer complex cases early. Vincristine/dactinomycin with or without doxorubicin are familiar Wilms regimens, but actual drugs, dose, schedule, infant adjustments and irradiation depend on stage, histology and COG/SIOP protocol. An isolated memorised dose is not a substitute for the named regimen.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [NCI PDQ: Wilms and other childhood kidney tumours](https://www.cancer.gov/types/kidney/hp/wilms-treatment-pdq)
- [Rationale for UMBRELLA SIOP-RTSG 2016](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrurol.2017.163.pdf)

questions.title: Neonatal obstruction and meconium ileus
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neonatal obstruction and meconium ileus

Failure to pass meconium with distension can reflect Hirschsprung disease, meconium ileus, meconium plug/small-left-colon syndrome, intestinal atresia, anorectal malformation, hypothyroidism, prematurity or sepsis-related ileus. Verify that the anus is anatomically normal and patent, document vomiting and examine for perforation or peritonitis.

Meconium ileus is distal small-bowel obstruction by inspissated meconium, commonly associated with cystic fibrosis through defective CFTR-mediated secretion. Simple disease has obstruction without vascular/perforation complications; complex disease includes volvulus, atresia, perforation and meconium peritonitis. Radiographs show dilated loops and a granular/soap-bubble appearance; calcification suggests antenatal perforation. A contrast enema can show microcolon and filling defects, and may reflux into the terminal ileum. Assess CF with sweat testing when technically feasible and/or CFTR testing; a neonatal bowel presentation must not be considered excluded by one limited mutation panel.

Resuscitate, keep warm, decompress and correct fluid/electrolyte deficits. In uncomplicated disease, a carefully performed water-soluble contrast enema under imaging can be diagnostic and therapeutic. Use an appropriately diluted agent, low controlled pressure, adequate hydration and close monitoring; stop if perforation or deterioration occurs. Hyperosmolar agents can cause major fluid shifts. Repeated controlled attempts may be reasonable in an otherwise stable child; perforation, ischaemia, complex obstruction or failure requires surgery.

Operative options include enterotomy and irrigation, limited resection with primary anastomosis in selected cases, or a stoma/Bishop-Koop/Santulli-type arrangement when bowel condition and instability warrant it. Minimise bowel loss. Postoperatively address pancreatic insufficiency, nutritional growth, fat-soluble vitamins and pulmonary CF care. Long-term prognosis depends substantially on the underlying CF phenotype and multidisciplinary care, rather than only the bowel operation.

### Intestinal rotation, malrotation and midgut volvulus

The midgut elongates, herniates physiologically into the umbilical cord around week 6 and rotates approximately 270 degrees counterclockwise around the SMA, viewed from the front, during herniation and return around week 10. Subsequent fixation places the duodenojejunal junction left of the spine and the caecum in the right lower quadrant, producing a broad mesenteric base. Nonrotation, incomplete rotation and abnormal fixation leave a narrow base and obstructing peritoneal bands; reversed rotation and internal hernia variants occur.

Bilious vomiting in a neonate demands urgent exclusion of volvulus. Older children may have intermittent pain/vomiting, poor growth or acute ischaemia. Stable patients usually undergo an upper-GI contrast study to locate the duodenojejunal junction and identify a corkscrew appearance. Ultrasound may show abnormal SMA/SMV relation and a whirlpool of mesentery/SMV around the SMA; vessel inversion alone is not definitive. In shock, peritonitis or strong evidence of ischaemic volvulus, resuscitation and surgery must not be delayed for a complete imaging sequence.

Keep nil by mouth; decompress stomach, obtain IV/IO access, restore perfusion, administer antibiotics for suspected ischaemia, and monitor lactate/electrolytes. At operation inspect viability, detorse the usual clockwise volvulus counterclockwise, divide Ladd bands, mobilise the duodenum/right colon and broaden the mesenteric base. Place small bowel predominantly on the right and colon on the left; appendicectomy is commonly performed because the caecum remains ectopic. The Ladd procedure does not restore normal embryological rotation. Reassess questionable bowel after reperfusion; preserve length and consider a planned second look rather than aggressive removal of potentially recoverable intestine.

Laparoscopy is feasible for stable selected cases, but gross distension, suspected ischaemia or instability may favour open surgery. Ensure mesenteric broadening is adequate. Long-term problems include adhesive obstruction, rare recurrent volvulus, persistent symptoms and short bowel after extensive resection. Families should seek immediate assessment for recurrent bilious vomiting.

![Original teaching schematic: malrotation. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/malrotation.svg)

questions.title: Antenatal hydronephrosis, UPJ obstruction and biomarkers
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Antenatal hydronephrosis, UPJ obstruction and biomarkers

Antenatal urinary-tract dilatation is an imaging finding, not a diagnosis. Record pelvic AP diameter, calyceal involvement, parenchymal thickness/echogenicity, ureter and bladder findings, amniotic fluid and laterality; use a UTD/SFU risk system rather than diameter alone. Consider transient dilatation, UPJ obstruction, VUR, duplex/ureterocele, UVJ obstruction and lower-tract obstruction.

Postnatal ultrasound is generally performed after early physiological dehydration has resolved; severe bilateral disease, solitary kidney or suspected LUTO needs earlier assessment. Evaluate urine infection and renal function in high-risk cases. VCUG is selected for ureteral/bladder abnormalities, suspected outlet obstruction or meaningful reflux risk; it is not obligatory in every isolated mild UPJ dilatation. Diuretic renography assesses differential renal function and drainage when the result affects management. Serial ultrasound and function trends distinguish stable nonobstructive dilatation from progressive obstruction.

Observe asymptomatic stable kidneys with preserved function. Consider pyeloplasty for pain/recurrent infection, progressive dilatation with thinning, impaired differential function or a sustained decline on serial evaluation. A low-function kidney should be judged with anatomy, test reliability, age and contralateral status. Anderson-Hynes dismembered pyeloplasty excises the narrowed segment, spatulates the ureter and creates a dependent tension-free anastomosis; address a crossing vessel without compromising its supply. Open, laparoscopic or robotic approaches depend on size and expertise. Follow postoperative symptoms, ultrasound and selected functional reassessment.

Urinary NGAL, KIM-1, MCP-1 and other proposed obstruction/fibrosis biomarkers remain adjunctive/research tools; assay variation, infection and age limit specificity. They do not replace ultrasound, functional studies or renal-function monitoring. In PUV, creatinine trend/nadir, BP, proteinuria and established function measures remain clinically important. When discussing recent biomarkers, separate promising association from validated routine decision criteria.

### Renal scintigraphy, diuretic renography and L,L-EC

99mTc-MAG3 is extracted predominantly by proximal tubular secretion and provides good images at lower renal function; 99mTc-L,L-ethylenedicysteine (EC) is another tubular agent. 99mTc-DTPA is filtered at the glomerulus and can estimate GFR but has lower extraction. 99mTc-DMSA is retained in renal cortex and is used for cortical anatomy/scarring and relative cortical function; it is not the usual drainage agent. The paper's 'LLEC scan' is interpreted as L,L-EC renal scintigraphy, rather than an unrelated test.

For a diuretic study, ensure hydration, review prior anatomy, select an age/weight-adjusted tracer activity and avoid a distended bladder; catheterization is selected for reflux, neurogenic bladder or drainage concerns. Dynamic images document perfusion, uptake and excretion. Furosemide increases urine flow, with F-0 or F+20-type protocols selected by the service. Quantify differential function, time-activity curves, drainage after diuretic, cortical transit and postvoid/gravity-assisted drainage.

Prompt washout argues against significant obstruction. Delayed washout can arise from obstruction, a very large compliant reservoir, dehydration, poor renal function or a full bladder. Traditional half-time categories (under 10 minutes reassuring, over 20 minutes potentially obstructed) must be interpreted with the whole study; half-time alone is not a diagnosis. Compare serial studies using similar technique. Draw a normal descending curve and an obstructed rising/plateau curve after diuretic, labelled as illustrative.

Captopril renography investigates suspected renovascular hypertension by reducing angiotensin-II-mediated efferent arteriolar support of filtration; a stenotic kidney may show reduced uptake/function and delayed transit after ACE inhibition. It has limited sensitivity in bilateral disease, small children and impaired renal function, and requires BP/safety monitoring. Other indications for isotope imaging include differential function before reconstructive surgery, ectopic/duplex anatomy, cortical scars and transplant perfusion/function.

### Duplex systems, ectopic ureter, ureterocele and megaureter

Complete duplication results from two ureteric buds; incomplete duplication from early division of one bud. By the Weigert-Meyer rule, the upper-moiety ureter generally opens inferomedially and is prone to ectopia/ureterocele or obstruction; the lower-moiety ureter opens superolaterally and is prone to reflux. Exceptions exist. A girl who dribbles continuously despite normal voluntary voiding suggests an ectopic ureter opening below the external sphincter; ordinary enuresis is intermittent. Boys' ectopic ureters usually open above the sphincter and cause infection/obstruction rather than continuous leakage.

Assess ultrasound, urine culture, renal function and moiety function. MR urography maps complex anatomy/ectopic insertion; VCUG evaluates reflux and urethra; DMSA or dynamic imaging measures function, while cystoscopy/vaginoscopy can identify outlets. A poorly functioning upper moiety can be treated by upper-pole heminephrectomy with careful preservation of lower-pole blood supply, or by ureteroureterostomy in suitable anatomy. A functioning moiety favours drainage-preserving reconstruction such as ureteroureterostomy or reimplantation. In the stated example with 3% upper and 36% lower function, do not sacrifice the functioning lower moiety; discuss upper-pole surgery versus drainage reconstruction based on anatomy, infections and tissue quality.

A ureterocele is cystic dilatation of the intravesical distal ureter; developmental theories include persistence of Chwalla's membrane and abnormal ureteral incorporation. Classify intravesical versus ectopic, single versus duplex. Cecoureterocele extends into/beyond the bladder neck. Infection, obstruction or retention may require endoscopic incision/puncture for decompression, followed by assessment for induced/persistent reflux and definitive reconstruction. Preserve functioning moieties and consider the bladder-neck effect.

Megaureter is a dilated ureter, commonly described as over 7 mm; categories are obstructed, refluxing, both, or nonobstructed/nonrefluxing, and primary versus secondary. Assess distal obstruction, VUR, bladder dysfunction and renal function with ultrasound, VCUG when indicated and renography. Many primary nonrefluxing cases improve with observation; recurrent febrile infections, symptoms, worsening dilatation or declining function favour intervention. Definitive reimplantation may require tapering, preserving adventitial blood supply. Temporizing drainage is useful in selected infants.

![Original teaching schematic: renogram. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/renogram.svg)

![Original teaching schematic: duplex law. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/duplex-law.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [EAU Guidelines on Paediatric Urology (2026)](https://uroweb.org/guidelines/paediatric-urology)
- [SNMMI/EANM paediatric diuresis renography guideline](https://snmmi.org/Web/Clinical-Practice/Procedure-Standards/Standards/Diuresis-Renography-in-Infants-and-Children.aspx)

questions.title: Necrotising enterocolitis
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Necrotising enterocolitis

NEC results from interacting prematurity, intestinal barrier/immune immaturity, dysbiosis, feeding and perfusion injury. Excess inflammatory signalling, including TLR4-associated responses, cytokines and impaired repair contributes; it is not simply infection by one organism. Distinguish spontaneous intestinal perforation, which may present differently in extremely preterm infants.

Modified Bell staging: I suspected disease with feeding intolerance/distension and nonspecific systemic signs; II definite disease with characteristic intestinal findings such as pneumatosis (IIA) and more severe systemic/laboratory disease/portal gas or ascites (IIB); III advanced disease with severe instability, coagulopathy and peritonitis (IIIA without, IIIB with perforation). Radiographs may show pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas, persistent dilated loops and free air. Ultrasound adds perfusion, wall thickness, portal gas and complex free fluid.

Stop feeds, decompress stomach, obtain cultures, start broad antimicrobial treatment according to local neonatal microbiology, support fluids/electrolytes/perfusion and respiratory function, and give PN when required. Serial examination, imaging, platelet count, lactate and acid-base trends matter more than one normal film. Free intraperitoneal air is a strong surgical indication; worsening clinical disease with suspected necrotic bowel, refractory shock, abdominal wall changes or deteriorating metabolic parameters may justify intervention without visible free air.

Laparotomy identifies necrosis, preserves viable bowel and provides resection with stoma or selected primary anastomosis. Peritoneal drainage is used in selected very small/unstable infants, with ongoing reassessment for definitive surgery; it is not necessarily curative. Pan-NEC involving nearly all bowel demands careful viability assessment, family discussion and bowel-preserving judgement; indiscriminate resection can create irreversible intestinal failure. Late problems include strictures (often colonic), short bowel, adhesions, cholestasis, growth and neurodevelopmental impairment. Persistent obstruction after recovery requires stricture evaluation.

### Cytokines and repair
Excess TNF-alpha, IL-1/IL-6-related inflammatory responses, endothelial injury and impaired epithelial repair can amplify NEC after microbial and perfusion insults in immature bowel. Growth/repair signals such as EGF influence mucosal resilience; breast-milk-associated protective factors and altered microbiota are part of the biological context. These mechanisms do not justify giving an unvalidated cytokine inhibitor or growth factor as routine neonatal therapy.

### IHPS and vomiting-related metabolic abnormalities

Infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis causes progressive nonbilious vomiting, dehydration and growth failure, typically in early infancy. Ultrasound evaluates pyloric thickness, channel length and gastric emptying using age/size-aware interpretation; an equivocal examination should not force a diagnosis. Bilious vomiting needs a different urgent pathway.

Loss of gastric hydrochloric acid causes hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis; volume contraction activates renin-aldosterone mechanisms, worsening potassium and hydrogen loss. Potassium may initially appear normal despite total-body depletion. The kidney first excretes bicarbonate; with profound chloride/volume and potassium depletion it retains sodium while secreting hydrogen, producing paradoxical aciduria despite systemic alkalosis. Alkalosis can depress ventilation, making anaesthesia unsafe before correction.

Decompress the stomach, use isotonic chloride-containing resuscitation with repeated assessment, then a maintenance/deficit plan with glucose and potassium only after urine output and potassium status are appropriate. Monitor chloride, potassium, bicarbonate, glucose and perfusion; satisfactory hydration, urine output and near-normal acid-base status are prerequisites to pyloromyotomy. It is a medical-resuscitation priority before an elective corrective operation, not an immediate unresuscitated surgical emergency.

Ramstedt pyloromyotomy splits the hypertrophied muscle from gastric to duodenal end while preserving mucosa; ensure an adequate complete myotomy and check for mucosal injury. Open or laparoscopic approaches are acceptable with appropriate expertise. Postoperative vomiting can be transient; persistent symptoms require evaluation for incomplete myotomy, mucosal injury or another diagnosis. Prepyloric vomiting favours acid loss/alkalosis; more distal obstruction can add bile/intestinal fluid losses, dehydration, mixed electrolyte depletion and acidosis if hypoperfusion/sepsis occurs. Do not assume every prolonged upper-GI obstruction has an identical chemistry profile.

### Preoperative correction and operative pitfalls
Review an initially 'normal' potassium with caution: alkalosis and aldosterone-related urinary loss can hide total-body depletion. Chloride replacement restores bicarbonate excretion, while improved perfusion and potassium repletion interrupt the cycle that produces paradoxical aciduria. Use serial venous chemistry/gases, fluid balance and clinical assessment to determine readiness rather than a single fluid bolus. Give appropriate dextrose maintenance for fasting infants and measure glucose; add potassium after urine flow and current chemistry are satisfactory. Local anaesthetic pathways specify exact bicarbonate/chloride targets and should be followed consistently.

A longitudinal myotomy is extended from the antral side to the duodenal end of the hypertrophied muscle, carefully spreading fibres so intact mucosa bulges without injury. The duodenal end is particularly susceptible to perforation; inspect when testing the myotomy. A perforation requires immediate recognized repair and a safe alternative myotomy/recovery plan under the operating team. Incomplete muscle division is a cause of persistent obstruction. Early postoperative feeding is protocol dependent; repeated vomiting with dehydration or failure to improve needs reassessment rather than unlimited reassurance. Include postoperative pain, hydration and follow-up counselling alongside the surgical step.

questions.title: Ventilation, ECMO and neonatal surgical intensive care
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Ventilation, ECMO and neonatal surgical intensive care

Ventilation options include pressure- or volume-targeted conventional modes, assist-control, SIMV with selected pressure support, and noninvasive support such as CPAP/NIPPV for appropriate patients. CPAP provides distending pressure without obligatory tidal breaths, recruiting lung and reducing work of breathing; it is not suitable for every apnoeic or obstructed infant. High-frequency oscillatory ventilation uses very small tidal volumes around a continuous distending pressure, with oxygenation largely influenced by lung recruitment/mean airway pressure and ventilation by oscillatory amplitude/frequency. High-frequency jet ventilation is a different system.

Choose settings by disease, lung mechanics and gases, aiming to avoid volutrauma, barotrauma, oxygen toxicity and haemodynamic compromise. HF modes can be used for selected air leaks and difficult oxygenation, including rescue in CDH, but excessive mean airway pressure can overdistend lungs and impair venous return. Mechanical ventilation risks include pneumothorax, ventilator-associated infection, chronic lung injury, airway trauma and adverse venous return. Weaning considers improving disease, adequate spontaneous drive, low support, stable gas exchange/perfusion, secretion handling and airway status; an isolated acceptable blood gas is insufficient.

ECMO uses a pump, membrane oxygenator and vascular cannulae to support gas exchange, with anticoagulation and close neurological/haematological surveillance. Veno-venous circuits principally support respiration; veno-arterial circuits support both circulation and respiration. Eligibility depends on reversible severe disease, size/gestation, bleeding/CNS risk and centre resources. CDH with refractory cardiopulmonary failure is a principal surgical-neonatal application; severe respiratory failure, selected sepsis/cardiac failure and perioperative support are others. ECMO does not reverse intrinsic pulmonary hypoplasia and has substantial bleeding, thrombosis, neurological and infectious risks. Timing of CDH repair on versus after ECMO is centre/protocol dependent.

A surgical NICU needs trained neonatal nurses and neonatology/surgery/anaesthesia teams, reliable warming, respiratory/haemodynamic monitoring, blood-gas and imaging support, infusion pumps, safe vascular access, PN, infection control, emergency equipment and access to blood products. Provide family support, pain management, transport links and follow-up. Staffing and protocols are as important as a list of machines.

### Respiratory-distress differential
Medical causes include surfactant-deficient RDS, transient tachypnoea, pneumonia/sepsis, pulmonary hypertension and congenital cardiac disease. Surgical/anatomical causes include CDH, CPAM/sequestration or lobar overinflation, airway obstruction/neck mass, EA-TEF-related aspiration, pneumothorax and major thoracic lesions. Distinguish an oxygenation problem from inadequate ventilation or a mechanical obstruction; bedside examination, radiograph, gases and echocardiography are selected by stability and suspected cause.

### Blood-product complications and monitored replacement

Immediate problems include wrong-patient/ABO incompatibility and acute haemolysis, febrile nonhaemolytic reactions, allergic reactions/anaphylaxis, bacterial contamination, circulatory overload and transfusion-related acute lung injury. Massive/rapid replacement can cause hypothermia, citrate-associated hypocalcaemia, potassium abnormalities, dilutional coagulopathy and acid-base disturbance. Neonates are particularly vulnerable to volume, temperature and metabolic shifts. Delayed problems include alloimmunisation, delayed haemolysis, iron overload with repeated transfusion, infection transmission and selected transfusion-associated GVHD risk.

Prevent avoidable harm by confirming patient identity, indication, product compatibility, special product requirements, access and baseline observations. Use an age/weight-appropriate rate and volume with measured response; warming and calcium monitoring are especially important during major replacement. In haemorrhagic shock, activate the local massive-transfusion pathway and address source control rather than repeatedly infuse crystalloid. Follow perfusion, haemoglobin, platelets/coagulation, ionised calcium, potassium and temperature. A haemoglobin concentration obtained during acute bleeding must be interpreted with timing and volume status.

If a suspected reaction occurs, stop the transfusion, maintain IV access with appropriate fluid, reassess airway/perfusion and verify patient/product details. Notify the transfusion service and obtain the investigations specified by the reaction protocol, including cultures for suspected contamination and haemolysis testing when indicated. Anaphylaxis, shock or respiratory failure needs immediate clinical treatment. Distinguish overload (volume-related cardiopulmonary findings) from TRALI (acute noncardiogenic lung injury), while recognizing that bedside differentiation may require detailed assessment.

Red-cell replacement restores oxygen-carrying capacity; plasma, platelets and fibrinogen-containing products address specific haemostatic deficits and are not general nutritional volume expanders. Irradiated, leukocyte-reduced and other specially selected components depend on immunological risk and the patient context. Document the reaction, future product precautions and whether the ongoing transfusion indication remains. In an examination, separate immunological, infectious and metabolic/volume complications before listing examples.

questions.title: Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Congenital diaphragmatic hernia: embryology, prognostication and stabilization

### Development and types
The diaphragm develops from the septum transversum (central tendon), paired pleuroperitoneal folds, dorsal mesentery of the oesophagus (crura), and muscular ingrowth from the body wall. Its descent explains the phrenic nerve supply from C3-C5. A simple failure-of-closure account is incomplete: abnormal pleuroperitoneal-fold mesenchyme and disturbed muscle development contribute to the defect; pulmonary hypoplasia may precede and then be aggravated by herniation (dual-hit model).

Bochdalek defects are posterolateral, usually left sided; Morgagni defects are anterior/retrosternal; central tendon defects are uncommon. Eventration is an intact but deficiently muscular diaphragm, rather than a true hole. Distinguish a hiatal hernia through the oesophageal hiatus from CDH. Label the heart, liver, bowel, lung and defect in a schematic.

### Antenatal assessment
Ultrasound shows intrathoracic stomach/bowel, mediastinal shift and a small ipsilateral lung. Assess side, liver position, observed-to-expected lung-to-head ratio (o/e LHR), defect severity, associated cardiac/genetic abnormalities and polyhydramnios. Fetal MRI estimates total fetal lung volume and liver herniation. Large defects, liver up, low o/e LHR or lung volume, and major associated anomalies worsen prognosis. Postnatally, pulmonary hypertension, ventricular dysfunction, oxygen requirement, oxygenation index and ECMO requirement add physiological information. Survival figures must specify whether they describe all diagnosed pregnancies, live births or treated infants.

### Immediate and intensive care management
Plan delivery in a centre with neonatal intensive care and paediatric surgery. Intubate a symptomatic known-CDH neonate and decompress the stomach with an orogastric tube; bag-mask ventilation can inflate intrathoracic bowel. Maintain warmth, analgesia and careful handling. Use gentle pressure-limited ventilation; avoid volutrauma and accept appropriate permissive hypercapnia while following pH, lactate and perfusion. Conventional ventilation is commonly first line; high-frequency ventilation is a rescue option when acceptable gas exchange cannot be obtained within safe pressures. Titrate oxygen to preductal saturation and assess pre/postductal difference. Echocardiography defines pulmonary hypertension and biventricular function; pulmonary vasodilators and vasoactive drugs should follow that physiology, rather than be given automatically.

Give cautious isotonic fluid aliquots with reassessment; excessive fluid worsens pulmonary oedema. Monitor arterial gases, BP, lactate trend, urine output, electrolytes and echocardiography. Refractory cardiopulmonary failure may require ECMO in an eligible infant. Repair follows physiological stabilization, rather than an arbitrary time after birth: acceptable oxygenation/ventilation on stable settings, satisfactory BP and urine output, improving lactate and controlled pulmonary hypertension. Reduce viscera and obtain tension-free closure; use a patch for a large defect. Severe physiology and large defects favour open repair; selected stable infants may undergo minimally invasive repair.

### Sudden acidosis and long-term issues
Check displaced/blocked tube, pneumothorax, worsening pulmonary hypertension, ventricular failure, sepsis, inadequate perfusion and bowel compromise. Check the circuit and tube, examine, obtain bedside imaging/echo and correct the cause promptly. Follow recurrence, pulmonary disease, reflux, growth, hearing and neurodevelopment. The historical shift is from urgent anatomical repair to lung-protective stabilization and delayed repair. FETO is a specialised option for selected severe fetal CDH, with prematurity and balloon-removal risks; it is not routine treatment for every fetus.

### Lung pathology and the management implication
Affected lungs have fewer/smaller airways and alveolar units and a reduced pulmonary vascular bed. Abnormal vascular muscularisation/reactivity contributes to high pulmonary vascular resistance, with right-heart pressure load and possible left-ventricular dysfunction. Consequently, high-pressure ventilation cannot simply 'inflate the missing lung'; overdistension of relatively preserved lung worsens injury and haemodynamics. Gentle ventilation, echocardiography-directed circulation support and delayed repair address this physiological disease alongside the anatomical defect.

### Omphalocele, gastroschisis, umbilical defects and complex associations

Omphalocele is a midline defect at the umbilical ring with a membrane covering bowel and sometimes liver; the cord inserts into the sac. It reflects disturbed ventral-body-wall development/return of herniated viscera and has important chromosomal, cardiac and syndromic associations. Gastroschisis is usually right paraumbilical, without a sac and with a separate cord; vascular and body-fold hypotheses exist, and a single established mechanism should not be claimed. Exposed bowel may become oedematous and matted. Hernia of the cord is a smaller, generally bowel-containing defect at the cord base; avoid clamping through bowel.

Ultrasound defines sac, liver, bowel appearance, cord insertion, growth and associated defects; offer genetic assessment especially for omphalocele. Counsel about delivery at a surgical centre, neonatal stabilization, possible staged closure and prolonged feeding recovery. Caesarean birth is not required for every abdominal-wall defect; giant liver-containing defects require individual planning.

At birth protect bowel/sac with sterile nonadherent material and a transparent bag, prevent heat loss, decompress stomach, establish access and replace fluid losses with measured reassessment. Avoid twisting the bowel pedicle and prolonged transport pressure. Gastroschisis can have primary closure if reduction does not compromise ventilation/perfusion; a preformed silo permits gradual reduction when visceroabdominal disproportion exists. Sutureless closure can use the umbilical remnant with dressings; possible benefits include less anaesthesia, with later umbilical hernia a trade-off. Complex gastroschisis with atresia/ischaemia/perforation requires individualized bowel preservation and staged treatment.

Giant omphalocele, particularly with liver and pulmonary hypoplasia, may require staged closure or delayed nonoperative epithelialisation ('paint and wait') followed by later reconstruction. Select topical agents carefully because of systemic absorption/toxicity. Monitor ventilation, abdominal pressure, urine output, limb perfusion, infection, PN-associated liver disease and growth. Primary closure must not be forced if it produces compartment physiology.

Cantrell pentalogy consists of a supraumbilical abdominal defect, lower sternal defect, anterior diaphragmatic defect, diaphragmatic pericardial defect and intracardiac abnormality. OEIS is omphalocele, cloacal exstrophy, imperforate anus and spinal defects. Both require cardiac, urological, spinal and intestinal mapping and staged multidisciplinary repair; preserve bowel, bladder plate, genital tissue and continence potential. Beckwith-Wiedemann spectrum involves 11p15 imprinting abnormalities, with macroglossia, overgrowth, abdominal-wall defect, hypoglycaemia and embryonal-tumour risk; surveillance follows the genetic subtype and regional recommendations.

### Paediatric trauma, FAST, solid-organ injury and emergency airway

Use a structured primary survey: airway with spinal protection, breathing, circulation/haemorrhage control, disability and exposure with warming; contemporary systems emphasise immediate control of catastrophic external haemorrhage. Children can maintain BP until late shock. Use age-appropriate equipment, IV/IO access, measured resuscitation and early blood for ongoing haemorrhage. Reassess after each intervention, then perform a secondary survey including safeguarding/history.

Airway tube size is age/weight dependent; common estimates for children beyond infancy are cuffed internal diameter age/4+3.5 mm or uncuffed age/4+4 mm, with adjacent sizes ready and confirmation by capnography, chest rise and depth checks. Neonates use gestation/weight charts; do not apply the older-child formula to them. Breathing threats include tension pneumothorax, open chest injury, haemothorax and lung contusion; treat life-threatening pathology promptly and provide adequate analgesia.

Four-view FAST assesses pericardium, right upper quadrant, left upper quadrant and pelvis for fluid; eFAST adds pleural assessment. A negative FAST does not exclude solid-organ or hollow-viscus injury in children. Stable patients with significant concern undergo contrast CT selected by clinical risk; unstable patients need haemorrhage control. Diagnostic peritoneal lavage historically identified intraperitoneal blood rapidly when imaging was unavailable, but is invasive, nonspecific and now rarely routine.

Most haemodynamically stable splenic, hepatic and renal injuries can be managed nonoperatively with serial examination and physiologic monitoring. ICU need, intervention and discharge are guided by clinical stability, not grade alone. Angioembolisation is selected for ongoing bleeding in a suitable patient; a CT blush alone is not a universal paediatric indication. Persistent instability despite blood or peritonitis requires operative assessment. Nonoperative risks include delayed bleeding, biloma/bile leak, missed bowel injury, urinoma and pseudoaneurysm. Use symptom-directed follow-up and an appropriate activity plan.

AAST grading broadly increases from minor capsular haematoma/laceration (I/II), deeper injury (III), major parenchymal/segmental vascular injury (IV), to shattered organ/hilar or major vascular injury (V); liver also has grade VI avulsion in the historical scale. Exact thresholds and the scale revision must be stated when reproducing a full grading table. Preserve splenic tissue when possible. After splenectomy, prevention of overwhelming infection includes pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib immunisation, appropriate antimicrobial prophylaxis, urgent fever assessment and medical-alert education; timing follows age and immune status.

![Original teaching schematic: trauma. Not to scale; use the accompanying text for clinical/operative detail.](assets/figures/trauma.svg)

#### Primary references and further reading

- [Canadian CDH Collaborative 2023 guideline update](https://fn.bmj.com/content/109/3/239)
- [ERNICA guidelines and endorsed statements](https://www.ern-ernica.eu/guidelines)
- [APSA updated blunt liver/spleen guidelines (2023 publication)](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=37117078)

questions.title: Neonatal thermoregulation, stress response and transport
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Neonatal thermoregulation, stress response and transport

Neonates lose heat through evaporation (wet skin), conduction (cold surfaces), convection (air currents) and radiation (nearby cold surfaces without contact). High surface-area-to-mass ratio, thin skin, limited insulation and prematurity increase vulnerability. Brown-fat nonshivering thermogenesis consumes oxygen and glucose; cold stress worsens hypoglycaemia, acidosis and pulmonary vascular resistance.

Dry term babies promptly, use a warmed environment, radiant warmer/incubator, prewarmed linens and a cap, minimise exposure and skin wetness, and use appropriately humidified/warmed respiratory support. Very preterm infants may benefit from polyethylene wrapping according to neonatal practice. During transfer use a warmed transport incubator with temperature, glucose, oxygenation and perfusion monitoring. During surgery maintain environmental warmth, warm fluids as appropriate, insulate exposed areas and monitor core temperature; exposed abdominal viscera create substantial evaporation. Avoid overheating and burns from unregulated heat sources.

The physiological response to injury includes an early ebb phase with shock-related low perfusion/metabolism, then a catabolic flow phase driven by catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and inflammatory mediators, followed by recovery/anabolism. Insulin resistance, proteolysis, lipolysis, nitrogen loss and fluid retention vary by severity and nutrition. Management controls pain, hypothermia, sepsis and hypoperfusion, uses appropriate nutrition and avoids overfeeding or tight glucose targets causing hypoglycaemia.

Postoperative neonatal thrombocytopenia can reflect sepsis/NEC, consumption/DIC, bleeding/dilution, drugs or immune causes. Assess trend, bleeding, coagulation, infection and sample artefact; treat the underlying disorder and use platelet support according to bleeding/procedural risk and neonatal thresholds, rather than automatically transfusing every low count. In a neonatal intensive-care plan, thermal care and glucose surveillance are core physiological interventions, not optional comfort measures.

### Paediatric/neonatal fluids, dehydration and electrolyte emergencies

Separate resuscitation, maintenance, pre-existing deficit and ongoing losses; these are not interchangeable. Estimate dehydration from examination and weight change where available. Deficit (mL) = body weight (kg) x percentage dehydration x 10. A 7-kg infant judged 7% dehydrated has an estimated 490-mL deficit; a 10-kg child at 10% has about 1000 mL, but the clinical estimate is imprecise. Severe peritonitis adds third-space losses, sepsis and possible haemorrhage. Use measured clinical response and serial chemistry to refine the plan.

For older infants/children, a common maintenance calculation is 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10, and 20 thereafter (the approximate hourly 4-2-1 rule). Neonatal needs differ with age, gestation, humidity, renal function and weight change. Typical term-neonate starting ranges rise from approximately 60-80 mL/kg/day on day 1 to 80-100 on day 2 and 100-120 on day 3; these are starting estimates, not fixed prescriptions for a sick surgical neonate. Prematurity, exposed bowel, phototherapy and losses change requirements. Use glucose-containing maintenance, introduce sodium/potassium according to adaptation, labs and urine output, and avoid blindly applying adult maintenance to neonates.

Shock requires isotonic resuscitation aliquots with frequent perfusion/lung/liver reassessment; choose blood early for haemorrhage. Fluid responsiveness and risk of overload determine further treatment. Replace NG/stoma/urinary losses by measured volume/composition and follow weight, balance, BP, capillary refill, glucose, sodium/potassium/chloride, gases and renal function. Correct hypernatraemic dehydration slowly under close monitoring; avoid rapid osmotic changes. Potassium is added only after renal function/urine output and serum potassium are assessed.

Hyperkalaemia: exclude haemolysed sampling if clinically safe, obtain ECG and assess renal failure, tissue injury, drugs and adrenal disease. Significant ECG changes/severe elevation need monitored IV calcium for membrane protection, insulin with glucose and selected beta-agonist to shift potassium, while stopping potassium input and correcting cause; dialysis may be needed for refractory renal failure. Calcium does not remove potassium. Hypocalcaemia requires ionised calcium interpretation, assessment of magnesium/phosphate and monitored calcium replacement if symptomatic; avoid extravasation and incompatible infusions. State age/weight units explicitly when using a local neonatal emergency-dose protocol.

questions.title: Branchial anomalies, thyroglossal tract and cervical lymphadenopathy
questions.body_md:
### Detailed revision answer

### Branchial anomalies, thyroglossal tract and cervical lymphadenopathy

The first arch forms jaws/masticatory structures and is supplied by CN V; the second forms stapes/styloid/stylohyoid and upper hyoid components with CN VII; the third forms lower hyoid components with CN IX; fourth/sixth arches contribute laryngeal cartilages/muscles with superior/recurrent laryngeal branches of CN X. The fifth is rudimentary. First pouch forms middle ear/auditory tube; second tonsillar epithelium; third thymus and inferior parathyroids; fourth superior parathyroids and ultimobranchial contribution. First cleft forms external auditory canal; remaining clefts are normally obliterated. First-arch syndromes include mandibulofacial abnormalities; assess airway and hearing.

Second-branchial fistula commonly extends from anterior SCM skin, between carotid branches, towards the tonsillar region; cysts can present as lateral neck swelling. First-cleft anomalies may track through parotid/external ear structures and require facial-nerve protection. Third/fourth pouch sinuses often reach the pyriform fossa and can cause recurrent, often left-sided, thyroid/neck infection; endoscopy and imaging help define them. Treat acute infection first, then excise the tract or perform selected endoscopic closure with protection of nearby nerves/vessels.

Thyroglossal remnants arise along thyroid descent from foramen caecum. Midline swelling moves with swallowing/tongue protrusion; suprahyoid, juxtahyoid and infrahyoid sites occur. Differential includes dermoid, ectopic thyroid, nodes and other cysts. Ultrasound confirms a normal thyroid and characterises the lesion; thyroid-function tests/scintigraphy are selected when ectopic-only thyroid is possible. Sistrunk excision removes cyst/tract, central hyoid and a core of tissue towards the tongue base. Simple cyst excision has high recurrence. Treat infection before elective repair.

Neck nodes: I submental/submandibular; II upper jugular; III middle jugular; IV lower jugular; V posterior triangle; VI central compartment; VII upper mediastinal. Persistent suspicious nodes require history/examination, ultrasound, CBC and targeted infection testing, then tissue sampling suitable for suspected pathology. Avoid corticosteroids before diagnostic sampling of possible lymphoma unless urgently necessary. Sialadenitis evaluation includes hydration, oral/dental findings, ultrasound and duct disease; chronic cases may need sialendoscopy. Do not remove ectopic thyroid without proving adequate alternative functioning thyroid.

### Operative detail for branchial fistula and Sistrunk
For a second-branchial tract, mark the external opening, use a skin-crease/selected step-ladder exposure, follow the tract through its anatomical path and protect hypoglossal/glossopharyngeal nerves and carotid vessels. Excise to the internal termination when safely defined; dye/probes are aids, not substitutes for anatomy. In Sistrunk surgery remove the central hyoid with the cyst and tract en bloc and a core of suprahyoid tissue directed towards the foramen caecum. Recurrence is associated with residual tract, inadequate hyoid/core excision or prior infection. Confirm normal thyroid before excising a possible sole ectopic thyroid.

### First-arch associations
Treacher Collins has mandibulofacial dysostosis with important airway/ear issues; hemifacial microsomia/Goldenhar spectrum involves variable craniofacial and vertebral/ocular abnormalities. Pierre Robin sequence has micrognathia with glossoptosis and often cleft palate, with airway/feeding implications. Distinguish these developmental syndromes from first-cleft fistulas through the parotid/ear region; they are not the same lesion category.

### Paediatric/neonatal fluids, dehydration and electrolyte emergencies

Separate resuscitation, maintenance, pre-existing deficit and ongoing losses; these are not interchangeable. Estimate dehydration from examination and weight change where available. Deficit (mL) = body weight (kg) x percentage dehydration x 10. A 7-kg infant judged 7% dehydrated has an estimated 490-mL deficit; a 10-kg child at 10% has about 1000 mL, but the clinical estimate is imprecise. Severe peritonitis adds third-space losses, sepsis and possible haemorrhage. Use measured clinical response and serial chemistry to refine the plan.

For older infants/children, a common maintenance calculation is 100 mL/kg/day for the first 10 kg, 50 for the next 10, and 20 thereafter (the approximate hourly 4-2-1 rule). Neonatal needs differ with age, gestation, humidity, renal function and weight change. Typical term-neonate starting ranges rise from approximately 60-80 mL/kg/day on day 1 to 80-100 on day 2 and 100-120 on day 3; these are starting estimates, not fixed prescriptions for a sick surgical neonate. Prematurity, exposed bowel, phototherapy and losses change requirements. Use glucose-containing maintenance, introduce sodium/potassium according to adaptation, labs and urine output, and avoid blindly applying adult maintenance to neonates.

Shock requires isotonic resuscitation aliquots with frequent perfusion/lung/liver reassessment; choose blood early for haemorrhage. Fluid responsiveness and risk of overload determine further treatment. Replace NG/stoma/urinary losses by measured volume/composition and follow weight, balance, BP, capillary refill, glucose, sodium/potassium/chloride, gases and renal function. Correct hypernatraemic dehydration slowly under close monitoring; avoid rapid osmotic changes. Potassium is added only after renal function/urine output and serum potassium are assessed.

Hyperkalaemia: exclude haemolysed sampling if clinically safe, obtain ECG and assess renal failure, tissue injury, drugs and adrenal disease. Significant ECG changes/severe elevation need monitored IV calcium for membrane protection, insulin with glucose and selected beta-agonist to shift potassium, while stopping potassium input and correcting cause; dialysis may be needed for refractory renal failure. Calcium does not remove potassium. Hypocalcaemia requires ionised calcium interpretation, assessment of magnesium/phosphate and monitored calcium replacement if symptomatic; avoid extravasation and incompatible infusions. State age/weight units explicitly when using a local neonatal emergency-dose protocol.

### Alimentary duplications, Meckel diverticulum and mesenteric lesions

Enteric duplications characteristically have alimentary epithelial lining, a smooth-muscle wall and close association/shared blood supply with native bowel. Cystic and tubular forms can occur anywhere; multiple developmental theories include abnormal recanalisation, split notochord and embryonic diverticula, none explaining every case. Ectopic gastric mucosa can bleed or ulcerate. Presentation includes prenatal/neonatal mass, obstruction, pain, bleeding, intussusception or infection. Ultrasound may show a double-wall/gut-signature sign; MRI/contrast studies map complex thoracic or pelvic lesions.

Resect the duplication with adjacent bowel when shared blood supply requires it; preserve length, especially for long tubular lesions, where mucosal stripping or tailored surgery may be considered. Rectal/colonic duplications need pelvic/urinary mapping; avoid sphincter, nerve and ureter injury. A cystic lymphatic malformation in the mesentery differs histologically from an enteric duplication; resection or selected sclerotherapy depends on relation to bowel vessels and symptoms.

Meckel diverticulum is a vitelline/omphalomesenteric-duct remnant on the antimesenteric ileal border. Remnants include patent duct, sinus, cyst, fibrous band and diverticulum. Complications include bleeding from ectopic gastric mucosa, inflammation, obstruction/bands, volvulus and intussusception. A 99mTc-pertechnetate scan detects functioning gastric mucosa rather than the diverticulum itself; fasting/appropriate preparation and selected acid-suppression protocols improve technique, but false results occur. Treat symptomatic disease with diverticulectomy or segmental ileal resection depending on base, inflammation and location of ectopic tissue.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (STK11) combines mucocutaneous pigmentation and hamartomatous polyps with obstruction/intussusception and cancer risk; surveillance and polyp clearance aim to preserve bowel. Familial adenomatous polyposis (APC) produces numerous adenomas and high colorectal-cancer risk; genetic counselling, lower/upper-GI surveillance and prophylactic colorectal surgery are individualized to polyp burden and extracolonic disease.

#### Primary references and further reading

- [Duke embryology: craniofacial development](https://embryology.oit.duke.edu/embryoModules/craniofacial/craniofacial.html)
